title: Seam Cutter
content:
Tool: Seam Cutter

I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image.

I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example.

title: Theatre Review: Opera UnTouched's "The Telephone" ★★★★★
content:
Why shouldn't an opera be set in an office? Not merely set there; performed there! On Saturday night, a couple of dozen audience members were ushered in to a genuine office in Tooting to watch a short comic opera by Opera UnTouched. It was a burst of sunshine in a rainy day.

We're at Ben's leaving party. A flustered woman is busy on the telephone. Will Ben ever get her attention?

Both Grace Watkins & Stephen Whitford are astonishingly good opera singers. They cover all the tropes, hit all the notes, and interact well with the audience.

I know that every production now claims it is immersive - but here, it genuinely is! The audience wanders through the set to get to the seats scattered around the office, there's a naff PowerPoint presentation projected on to the wall, a leaving card is waiting for us to sign, the singers prance among us.

Just intensely joyful.

My only real criticism it that it is too short! I suspect it is designed to be a pop-up experience, fringe show, or performed during a break in the corporate drudgery. I'd've gladly watched a full length production and traipsed through a series of office spaces to get the the next scene.

You can watch excerpts on Instagram.

Pre- and Post-Show

As I've written about before, theatrical shows need to do something special to warm up their audiences. Opera UnTouched had a tough job with an audience drenched in London's rain.

The "office manager" ushered us in to the space and told us that it was Ben's last day, so we were all welcome at his leaving drinks. It being a modern office, we were each given a lanyard to wear throughout the show (which also sneakily doubled as an audience feedback QR).

As it was a party, as we wandered round the office space, we were each handed a glass of Prosecco - what a lovely touch! There's a reason your Chinese takeaway comes with "free" prawn crackers; receiving a gift makes you feel cherished. For the cost of a few dozen reusable plastic flutes and all of about 73p worth of fizz each, the audience were positively beaming by the time the show started.

Why can't more shows do that? OK, it might eat in to the takings at the bar. But a welcome drink on arrival is such an easy way to win over the audience.

As for post-show, there was the obligatory plea to fill in the feedback form. Charmingly, after receiving rapturous applause, the cast and creatives came back and were happy to chat to the audience and discuss the show.

title: Where else to find me
content:
This blog is the main place I write, but I also use other platforms, either to write new content or to announce blog posts.

X (née Twitter)

I have a several X accounts, one personal account (@JohnDCook) and several specialized accounts (@CompSciFact, @AlgebraFact, @DataSciFact, etc.). I announce new blog posts on the most relevant account.

RSS

You can subscribe to the blog via RSS and find out about each post as it’s published.

RSS was very popular before Google killed its RSS reader, but it still works just fine. I use RSS to subscribe to the blogs I read.

The hard part of using RSS is finding a reader you like. I use Inoreader. I’m sure an LLM could help you find an RSS reader for your preferences and help you get started using it.

Mathstodon & Bluesky

I announce my math-related posts on Mathstodon at mathstodon.xyz/@johndcook. I also use a service that repeats my Mathstodon posts to Bluesky at johndcook.mathstodon.xyz.ap.brid.gy.

I don’t know why, but more people have started following me on Mathstodon over the last couple weeks.

Substack

Some people like to get email notifications of posts. I used two or three services that sent out such emails and they all stopped working. I tried out Substack and it has worked smoothly ever since.

My Substack newsletter has evolved into a bit more than just blog post announcements. I give a little intro to each post and some additional info such as how a sequence of posts are related or ideas that occurred to me after writing the post.

LinkedIn

Once in a while I post something to LinkedIn. If you’d like to know more about my background, you can see my profile there.

title: Package Management Devroom at FOSDEM 2027: Call for Participation
content:
Cross-posted from the Software Stewardship Lab.

The Package Management devroom is back at FOSDEM 2027, on Sunday 31 January from 13:15 to 17:00 at the Université libre de Bruxelles. The call for participation is open and submissions close on 1 December at 23:59 UTC, through pretalx.

Wolf Vollprecht and I ran the devroom at FOSDEM 2026 after putting out last year’s call for participation on the Ecosystems blog. The devroom had nine talks, listed in the schedule post and written up alongside the rest of the weekend’s package management content in Package Management at FOSDEM 2026. This year there are four of us, with Vlad Miricioiu from the Stewardship Lab, who spoke last year, and Travis Hathaway from Anaconda joining Wolf and me.

I’d happily take more talks like these from last year:

  • Matthew Suozzo showed how OSS Rebuild instruments the build environment, with a transparent network proxy and an eBPF-based system analyzer, to catch suspicious behaviour that a reproducible build check would pass.
  • Ryan Gibb presented the Package Calculus, a formal model of dependency resolution that reduces the features of different package managers to one core calculus.
  • Vlad Miricioiu covered binary dependencies that are missing from package manifests, like numpy’s reliance on OpenBLAS.
  • Adam Harvey walked through the phishing campaign against crates.io owners and how the Rust Project, Rust Foundation and Alpha-Omega shut it down.

We want talks from package manager and registry maintainers on the problems they keep running into: dependency resolution, namespaces, signing, reproducibility, metadata standards, cross-ecosystem dependencies, and this year’s new supply chain attacks. We’d especially like talks on under-discussed parts of package management rather than more AI-augmented security tooling, and from people and communities underrepresented in free and open source software.

Pick “Package Management” as the track when you submit. Talks are 20 minutes by default, and if you’d prefer a 10 minute slot, say so in the “Submission Notes” field and we should be able to fit it in. Include a list of related previous work and a short bio for each speaker. Submitting means agreeing to the FOSDEM Code of Conduct.

We’ll be in touch with selected speakers on 4 December, and the schedule will be published on 7 December. Send any questions about the devroom or your submission to package-management-devroom-manager@fosdem.org.

title: Why My Dad Didn’t Have a Cell Phone
content:
Here’s Dave Rupert writing about all those emails, texts, phone calls, etc. we’re getting these days:

Once upon a time it had utility, now it’s all noise and grifter slop demanding our attention and giving us to-dos

That last part really hit: “giving us to-dos”.

I feel this. So many of the messenger apps on my phone are other people laying claim to my time and attention.

It reminds me of an interaction I had with my Dad years ago.

This was back when cell phones were starting to become ubiquitous.

Not smartphones, mind you. Cell phones, i.e. telephones that were mobile. Texting wasn’t really a thing yet. These were devices for making voice calls wherever you went.

As a teen, it seemed like everyone had one: my teachers, my friends, even my friends’ parents.

But not my parents.

They were “behind the times”. (Everyone was getting cell phones and we didn’t even have caller ID on our landline!)

One night at family dinner I asked, “Dad, why don’t you have a cell phone?”

His response?

“Why would I want to allow other people to contact me whenever they want?”

I still think about that.
